text: We introduce scalable deep kernels, which combine the structural properties of deep learning architectures with the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods. Specifically, we transform the inputs of a spectral mixture base kernel with a deep architecture, using local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and structure exploiting (Kronecker and Toeplitz) algebra for a scalable kernel representation. We jointly learn the properties of these kernels through the marginal likelihood of a Gaussian process. Inference and learning cost $O(n)$ for $n$ training points, and predictions cost $O(1)$ per test point. text: We describe a seriation algorithm for ranking a set of items given pairwise comparisons between these items. Intuitively, the algorithm assigns similar rankings to items that compare similarly with all others. It does so by constructing a similarity matrix from pairwise comparisons, using seriation methods to reorder this matrix and construct a ranking. We first show that this spectral seriation algorithm recovers the true ranking when all pairwise comparisons are observed and consistent with a total order. We then show that ranking reconstruction is still exact when some pairwise comparisons are corrupted or missing, and that seriation based spectral ranking is more robust to noise than classical scoring methods. Finally, we bound the ranking error when only a random subset of the comparions are observed. An additional benefit of the seriation formulation is that it allows us to solve semi-supervised ranking problems. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that seriation based spectral ranking achieves competitive and in some cases superior performance compared to classical ranking methods.

text: Controller synthesis for hybrid systems that satisfy temporal specifications expressing various system properties is a challenging problem that has drawn the attention of many researchers. However, making the assumption that such temporal properties are deterministic is far from the reality. For example, many of the properties the controller has to satisfy are learned through machine learning techniques based on sensor input data. In this paper, we propose a new logic, Probabilistic Signal Temporal Logic (PrSTL), as an expressive language to define the stochastic properties, and enforce probabilistic guarantees on them. We further show how to synthesize safe controllers using this logic for cyber-physical systems under the assumption that the stochastic properties are based on a set of Gaussian random variables. One of the key distinguishing features of PrSTL is that the encoded logic is adaptive and changes as the system encounters additional data and updates its beliefs about the latent random variables that define the safety properties. We demonstrate our approach by synthesizing safe controllers under the PrSTL specifications for multiple case studies including control of quadrotors and autonomous vehicles in dynamic environments.

text: This paper presents our work on development of OWL-driven systems for formal representation and reasoning about terminological knowledge and facts in petrology. text: Relational data sources are still one of the most popular ways to store enterprise or Web data, however, the issue with relational schema is the lack of a well-defined semantic description. A common ontology provides a way to represent the meaning of a relational schema and can facilitate the integration of heterogeneous data sources within a domain. Semantic labeling is achieved by mapping attributes from the data sources to the classes and properties in the ontology. We formulate this problem as a multi-class classification problem where previously labeled data sources are used to learn rules for labeling new data sources. The majority of existing approaches for semantic labeling have focused on data integration challenges such as naming conflicts and semantic heterogeneity. In addition, machine learning approaches typically have issues around class imbalance, lack of labeled instances and relative importance of attributes. To address these issues, we develop a new machine learning model with engineered features as well as two deep learning models which do not require extensive feature engineering. We evaluate our new approaches with the state-of-the-art.

text: This work introduces computational methods for inducing interpretable two-level Boolean classifiers expressed in either CNF (AND-of-ORs) or DNF (OR-of-ANDs) representations, with the objective of balancing predictive performance against model interpretability. Two distinct optimization frameworks are presented. The first employs an integer programming formulation that minimizes a composite objective combining classification errors and feature utilization, extending an existing LP relaxation technique from single-level to two-level rule structures. The second approach substitutes the standard 0-1 loss with Hamming distance, measuring deviation from the nearest rule achieving perfect classification on each instance. From this alternative formulation, block coordinate descent and alternating minimization procedures are derived. Empirical results demonstrate that two-level rules substantially outperform their single-level counterparts by exploiting significantly increased expressive capacity, with the Hamming distance-based algorithms consistently achieving superior results relative to competing two-level rule learning approaches. Additionally, a post-processing technique for converting fractional components in LP relaxation solutions to binary values demonstrates practical effectiveness.

text: We present an end-to-end approach for automatically constructing task-oriented dialogue systems from minimal amounts of raw dialogue data. The method integrates an incremental semantic grammar framework—Dynamic Syntax and Type Theory with Records (DS-TTR)—with Reinforcement Learning (RL), treating language generation and dialogue management as a unified optimization problem. The resulting systems operate incrementally, processing dialogue at the word level, a property known to facilitate natural and spontaneous interactions. We posit that the expressive linguistic structure embedded in the grammar enables the system to handle a vast array of dialogue variations despite exposure to only a small training corpus. Our evaluation demonstrates that the model successfully processes 74% of the Facebook AI bAbI dataset when trained on merely 0.13% of available examples (5 dialogues). Furthermore, it handles 65% of bAbI+, a dataset we developed by systematically incorporating incremental dialogue phenomena including restarts and self-corrections into the original bAbI corpus. We provide a comparative analysis against MemN2N, a leading retrieval-based baseline, and demonstrate that MemN2N exhibits substantial performance degradation when encountering bAbI+ phenomena, even when trained on the complete bAbI dataset, whereas our approach maintains stronger semantic accuracy.

text: L1 regularisation has become a focal point of research on sparse learning, finding successful applications in fields ranging from signal acquisition and image coding to genomics and collaborative filtering. Although prior studies emphasise the many benefits of L1‑based approaches, we show that, in terms of predictive accuracy, L1 regularisation can fall far short of alternative sparsity‑inducing techniques. Concentrating on unsupervised latent‑variable models, we construct factor models that minimise an L1 penalty, Bayesian analogues of L1, and Bayesian factor models that impose a more stringent, L0‑like sparsity via spike‑and‑slab priors. The spike‑and‑slab Bayesian models promote sparsity while formally incorporating uncertainty and avoiding the excessive shrinkage of genuine non‑zero coefficients. Empirical evaluations on several data sets reveal that, even under comparable computational constraints, spike‑and‑slab Bayesian methods consistently surpass L1 minimisation in predictive performance. text: POMDPs are standard models for probabilistic planning problems, where an agent interacts with an uncertain environment. We study the problem of almost-sure reachability, where given a set of target states, the question is to decide whether there is a policy to ensure that the target set is reached with probability 1 (almost-surely). While in general the problem is EXPTIME-complete, in many practical cases policies with a small amount of memory suffice. Moreover, the existing solution to the problem is explicit, which first requires to construct explicitly an exponential reduction to a belief-support MDP. In this work, we first study the existence of observation-stationary strategies, which is NP-complete, and then small-memory strategies. We present a symbolic algorithm by an efficient encoding to SAT and using a SAT solver for the problem. We report experimental results demonstrating the scalability of our symbolic (SAT-based) approach.

The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) is a recently proposed test statistic for two-sample test. Its quadratic time complexity, however, greatly hampers its availability to large-scale applications. To accelerate the MMD calculation, in this study we propose an efficient method called FastMMD. The core idea of FastMMD is to equivalently transform the MMD with shift-invariant kernels into the amplitude expectation of a linear combination of sinusoid components based on Bochner's theorem and Fourier transform (Rahimi & Recht, 2007). Taking advantage of sampling of Fourier transform, FastMMD decreases the time complexity for MMD calculation from $O(N^2 d)$ to $O(L N d)$, where $N$ and $d$ are the size and dimension of the sample set, respectively. Here $L$ is the number of basis functions for approximating kernels which determines the approximation accuracy. For kernels that are spherically invariant, the computation can be further accelerated to $O(L N \log d)$ by using the Fastfood technique (Le et al., 2013). The uniform convergence of our method has also been theoretically proved in both unbiased and biased estimates. We have further provided a geometric explanation for our method, namely ensemble of circular discrepancy, which facilitates us to understand the insight of MMD, and is hopeful to help arouse more extensive metrics for assessing two-sample test. Experimental results substantiate that FastMMD is with similar accuracy as exact MMD, while with faster computation speed and lower variance than the existing MMD approximation methods.

It is assumed that the data set, to begin with, is endowed with a metric, and we include discussion of how this can be brought about if a dissimilarity, only, holds. Furthermore a major objective is to determine locally ultrametric relationships as opposed to non-local ultrametric relationships. text: In 1979 Stockman introduced the SSS* minimax search algorithm that domi- nates Alpha-Beta in the number of leaf nodes expanded. Further investigation of the algorithm showed that it had three serious drawbacks, which prevented its use by practitioners: it is difficult to understand, it has large memory requirements, and it is slow. This paper presents an alternate formulation of SSS*, in which it is implemented as a series of Alpha-Beta calls that use a transposition table (AB- SSS*). The reformulation solves all three perceived drawbacks of SSS*, making it a practical algorithm. Further, because the search is now based on Alpha-Beta, the extensive research on minimax search enhancements can be easily integrated into AB-SSS*. To test AB-SSS* in practise, it has been implemented in three state-of-the- art programs: for checkers, Othello and chess. AB-SSS* is comparable in performance to Alpha-Beta on leaf node count in all three games, making it a viable alternative to Alpha-Beta in practise. Whereas SSS* has usually been regarded as being entirely different from Alpha-Beta, it turns out to be just an Alpha-Beta enhancement, like null-window searching. This runs counter to published simulation results. Our research leads to the surprising result that iterative deepening versions of Alpha-Beta can expand fewer leaf nodes than iterative deepening versions of SSS* due to dynamic move re-ordering.

text: Complex networks refer to large-scale graphs with nontrivial connection patterns. The salient and interesting features that the complex network study offer in comparison to graph theory are the emphasis on the dynamical properties of the networks and the ability of inherently uncovering pattern formation of the vertices. In this paper, we present a hybrid data classification technique combining a low level and a high level classifier. The low level term can be equipped with any traditional classification techniques, which realize the classification task considering only physical features (e.g., geometrical or statistical features) of the input data. On the other hand, the high level term has the ability of detecting data patterns with semantic meanings. In this way, the classification is realized by means of the extraction of the underlying network's features constructed from the input data. As a result, the high level classification process measures the compliance of the test instances with the pattern formation of the training data. Out of various high level perspectives that can be utilized to capture semantic meaning, we utilize the dynamical features that are generated from a tourist walker in a networked environment. Specifically, a weighted combination of transient and cycle lengths generated by the tourist walk is employed for that end. Interestingly, our study shows that the proposed technique is able to further improve the already optimized performance of traditional classification techniques.

text: In this paper, we address referring expression comprehension: localizing an image region described by a natural language expression. While most recent work treats expressions as a single unit, we propose to decompose them into three modular components related to subject appearance, location, and relationship to other objects. This allows us to flexibly adapt to expressions containing different types of information in an end-to-end framework. In our model, which we call the Modular Attention Network (MAttNet), two types of attention are utilized: language-based attention that learns the module weights as well as the word/phrase attention that each module should focus on; and visual attention that allows the subject and relationship modules to focus on relevant image components. Module weights combine scores from all three modules dynamically to output an overall score. Experiments show that MAttNet outperforms previous state-of-art methods by a large margin on both bounding-box-level and pixel-level comprehension tasks. Demo and code are provided.

text: We consider infinite-horizon stationary $γ$-discounted Markov Decision Processes, for which it is known that there exists a stationary optimal policy. text: Consensus formation is investigated for multi-agent systems in which agents' beliefs are both vague and uncertain. Vagueness is represented by a third truth state meaning \emph{borderline}. This is combined with a probabilistic model of uncertainty. A belief combination operator is then proposed which exploits borderline truth values to enable agents with conflicting beliefs to reach a compromise. A number of simulation experiments are carried out in which agents apply this operator in pairwise interactions, under the bounded confidence restriction that the two agents' beliefs must be sufficiently consistent with each other before agreement can be reached. As well as studying the consensus operator in isolation we also investigate scenarios in which agents are influenced either directly or indirectly by the state of the world. For the former we conduct simulations which combine consensus formation with belief updating based on evidence. For the latter we investigate the effect of assuming that the closer an agent's beliefs are to the truth the more visible they are in the consensus building process. In all cases applying the consensus operators results in the population converging to a single shared belief which is both crisp and certain. Furthermore, simulations which combine consensus formation with evidential updating converge faster to a shared opinion which is closer to the actual state of the world than those in which beliefs are only changed as a result of directly receiving new evidence. Finally, if agent interactions are guided by belief quality measured as similarity to the true state of the world, then applying the consensus operator alone results in the population converging to a high quality shared belief.

text: For some computational problems (e.g., product configuration, planning, diagnosis, query answering, phylogeny reconstruction) computing a set of similar/diverse solutions may be desirable for better decision-making. With this motivation, we studied several decision/optimization versions of this problem in the context of Answer Set Programming (ASP), analyzed their computational complexity, and introduced offline/online methods to compute similar/diverse solutions of such computational problems with respect to a given distance function. All these methods rely on the idea of computing solutions to a problem by means of finding the answer sets for an ASP program that describes the problem. The offline methods compute all solutions in advance using the ASP formulation of the problem with an ASP solver, like Clasp, and then identify similar/diverse solutions using clustering methods. The online methods compute similar/diverse solutions following one of the three approaches: by reformulating the ASP representation of the problem to compute similar/diverse solutions at once using an ASP solver; by computing similar/diverse solutions iteratively (one after other) using an ASP solver; by modifying the search algorithm of an ASP solver to compute similar/diverse solutions incrementally. We modified Clasp to implement the last online method and called it Clasp-NK. In the first two online methods, the given distance function is represented in ASP; in the last one it is implemented in C++. We showed the applicability and the effectiveness of these methods on reconstruction of similar/diverse phylogenies for Indo-European languages, and on several planning problems in Blocks World. We observed that in terms of computational efficiency the last online method outperforms the others; also it allows us to compute similar/diverse solutions when the distance function cannot be represented in ASP.

text: We have previously reported a Bayesian algorithm for determining the coordinates of points in three-dimensional space from uncertain constraints. In this paper, we present an extension of the original algorithm that allows constraint uncertainty to be represented as a mixture of Gaussians, and thereby allows arbitrary constraint distributions.  We illustrate the performance of this algorithm on a problem drawn from the domain of molecular structure determination, in which a multicomponent constraint representation produces a much more accurate solution than the old single component mechanism.  The new mechanism uses mixture distributions to decompose the problem into a set of independent problems with unimodal constraint uncertainty.  The results of the unimodal subproblems are periodically recombined using Bayes' law, to avoid combinatorial explosion.  The new algorithm is particularly suited for parallel implementation.

text: In this paper we introduce the notion of Demand-Weighted Completeness, allowing estimation of the completeness of a knowledge base with respect to how it is used. Defining an entity by its classes, we employ usage data to predict the distribution over relations for that entity. For example, instances of person in a knowledge base may require a birth date, name and nationality to be considered complete. These predicted relation distributions enable detection of important gaps in the knowledge base, and define the required facts for unseen entities. Such characterisation of the knowledge base can also quantify how usage and completeness change over time. We demonstrate a method to measure Demand-Weighted Completeness, and show that a simple neural network model performs well at this prediction task.

The discipline of computer science that seeks to construct machines capable of exhibiting behaviors regarded as intelligent by humans has long fascinated scholars. From antiquity’s fascination with artificial cognition to the modern era of computers and five decades of research in diverse programming paradigms, the vision of truly intelligent machines is approaching practical realization. Contemporary researchers have developed systems that emulate human reasoning, comprehend spoken language, defeat world‑class chess champions, and accomplish numerous tasks previously thought unattainable. Human proficiency in processing information is most evident in the use of natural language, where linguistic terms are employed to evaluate qualitative attributes. Such evaluations inevitably introduce uncertainty in the form of vagueness. Consequently, vague sets, vague judgments, and vague conclusions arise whenever a rational agent is involved and expresses interest in a particular subject. Vague‑set theory emerged as a response to the inherent imprecision of human language. The language of a rational agent is generated by vague events produced by reasoning and processed by the mind. Vague‑set theory offers an approximation of these imprecise groupings that is more suitable than classical set theory in contexts where natural language plays a central role; this framework was introduced by the American mathematicians Gau and Buehrer. In the present paper we demonstrate how the vagueness of linguistic variables can be addressed through vague‑set theory. The work is situated within the domain of eventology—the theory of random vague events—developed within probability theory to provide an event‑theoretic description of the dynamics of reasoning.

text: Word reordering remains one of the most challenging components of statistical machine translation (SMT), profoundly influencing both translation quality and computational efficiency. Although a substantial body of research has been produced, the community’s interest in this issue persists, and no single technique has emerged as universally superior across different language pairs. Consequently, selecting the most appropriate method for a new translation task continues to rely heavily on empirical experimentation. To guide readers through this extensive and intricate field, we provide a thorough survey that treats word reordering both as a statistical modeling problem and as a linguistic phenomenon. The review details how reordering is represented in various string‑based and tree‑based SMT architectures, as well as in dedicated reordering tasks, offering systematic overviews of the literature on advanced reordering models. We then examine why certain approaches outperform others for specific language pairs. Beyond merely quantifying the amount of reordering, we argue that it is crucial to identify the particular types of reordering that arise in a given pair of languages. To this end, we perform a qualitative analysis of reordering phenomena across a diverse set of language pairs, drawing on an extensive repository of linguistic knowledge. Empirical findings from the SMT literature support the hypothesis that a small number of linguistic facts can reliably predict a language pair’s reordering behavior and help choose the SMT framework that best accommodates it.

text: Long Short‑Term Memory (LSTM) networks constitute a predominant recurrent architecture for modeling sequential data. Their design relies on gating mechanisms to regulate the flow of information—deciding, for instance, whether to retain or discard particular signals—yet conventional implementations based on soft (continuous) gates only approximate this principle. In this work we introduce a novel training paradigm that drives gate activations toward binary extremes (0 or 1). Consequently, the gates are predominantly either fully open or fully closed, reducing ambiguous intermediate states and enhancing interpretability of the information pathway. Extensive experiments demonstrate that: (1) despite an apparent reduction in model flexibility, performance does not deteriorate; in fact, the binary‑biased models achieve equal or superior results owing to improved generalization, and (2) gate outputs become largely insensitive to their inputs, enabling straightforward compression of LSTM units via techniques such as low‑rank and low‑precision approximations. text: This paper presents a probabilistic framework that unifies Markov random fields of bounded treewidth with probabilistic context-free grammars. These models utilize case-factor diagrams (CFDs), a specialized representation for Boolean formulas. text: In this work, we establish theoretical connections between Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) and Bayesian Networks (BNs). We prove that every SPN can be transformed into a BN in time and space linear in the size of the network. The central idea is to employ Algebraic Decision Diagrams (ADDs) to compactly encode the local conditional probability distributions at each BN node by exploiting context-specific independence (CSI). text: We present two new nonparametric statistical hypothesis tests. The first, called the relative dependency test, evaluates whether one source variable is significantly more dependent on a first target variable than on a second. Dependence is quantified by the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC). The second, called the relative similarity test, determines which of two samples from arbitrary distributions is significantly closer to a reference sample, with the relative similarity quantified by the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). To construct these tests, we use as test statistics the differences of HSIC statistics and of MMD statistics, respectively. The resulting tests are consistent and unbiased and exhibit favorable convergence properties. The effectiveness of the relative dependency test is demonstrated on several real-world problems: identifying language groups from a multilingual parallel corpus and showing that tumor location is more dependent on gene expression than on chromosome imbalance. We also illustrate the performance of the relative test of similarity over a broad selection of model comparison problems in deep generative models.

text: Coalition formation is a fundamental interaction that entails constructing coherent groups of distinct, autonomous agents in order to efficiently pursue their individual or shared objectives. A central challenge in multi-agent systems is determining which coalitions to form to achieve a given goal, which typically requires assigning a coalition value to each possible coalition to indicate the benefit of its formation. After these values are computed, agents must assemble a partition of the agent set into coalitions—each agent belonging to exactly one coalition—that maximizes the overall system outcome. The coalition structure generation problem is exceedingly difficult because the number of potential structures grows exponentially with the number of agents. Consequently, a variety of algorithms—ranging from dynamic programming and integer programming to stochastic search—have been proposed, yet all suffer from notable limitations in execution time, solution quality, or memory consumption. To address this, we develop an anytime algorithm for the coalition structure generation problem. The approach introduces a novel representation of the search space that partitions feasible solutions into subspaces, enabling computation of upper and lower bounds on the values of the best coalition structures within each subspace. These bounds are used to prune subspaces that cannot contain the optimal solution. The remaining subspaces are explored with a branch-and-bound strategy, efficiently traversing them without exhaustively enumerating all solutions within the examined regions. We prove that the algorithm enumerates all coalition structures efficiently by automatically discarding redundant and invalid solutions. To assess the method, we also introduce a new input distribution designed to yield more reliable benchmarks than those previously used in the literature. Under this distribution, for 27 agents our algorithm finds optimal solutions in only 0.175% of the time required by the fastest algorithm reported in the literature. The algorithm is anytime: if interrupted before its usual termination, it still delivers a solution with a provable bound relative to the optimum. Moreover, the guarantees on solution quality are substantially better than those of prior state-of-the-art approaches. For example, on a worst-case distribution with 25 agents, the method achieves a solution that is 90% efficient in roughly 10% of the time required to obtain the optimum.

text: Statistical null hypotheses are standard in the hard sciences but have seen limited use in theoretical linguistics. Here the null hypothesis that a low frequency of syntactic dependency crossings arises from an arbitrary word order is rejected. It is shown that accepting such a null would require star-shaped dependency structures, which are unrealistic and overly restrictive. The hypothesis of limited cognitive resources in the human brain is reevaluated. Stronger null hypotheses that incorporate actual dependency lengths when assessing the likelihood of crossings are introduced. These hypotheses suggest that crossings become less likely as dependency lengths shorten. A hypothesis based on pressure to reduce dependency lengths is more parsimonious than a principle of crossing minimization or a grammatical ban that is completely dissociated from the general, non-linguistic principle of economy.

text: Nicod's criterion posits that observing a black raven provides evidence for the hypothesis H that all ravens are black. We show that Solomonoff induction does not conform to Nicod's criterion: there exist time steps in which observing black ravens reduces the posterior probability of H. We argue that the fault lies not with Solomonoff induction itself, but with Nicod's criterion, which should be abandoned.

text: Punctuation serves as a reliable marker of syntactic organization, and parsers developed on conventionally punctuated text typically depend substantially on this feature. Yet this dependence is problematic, as human language comprehension does not utilize punctuation to the same degree, and informal writing frequently omits it altogether. Additionally, punctuation is sometimes employed in non-standard ways for stylistic emphasis, creative expression, or simply through error. This work demonstrates that (a) dependency parsers exhibit vulnerability to both the removal of punctuation and its unconventional application; (b) neural-based parsers display greater susceptibility than traditional parsing approaches; (c) neural parsers trained on unpunctuated text achieve superior performance compared to standard pre-trained parsers in all cases involving non-standard punctuation usage. The primary analysis employs artificially modified datasets to isolate punctuation effects while minimizing confounding variables, supplemented by evaluation on authentic out-of-domain text.

text: Managing knowledge base reasoning systems presents significant difficulties when dealing with pervasive ontological uncertainty and temporally uncertain updates, particularly when balancing performance requirements against computational efficiency. This work introduces a domain-agnostic approach for integrating ontologies within open, interactive environments. We present a framework combining Multi-Entity Bayesian Networks with SWRL rules, implemented through a Java application, that continuously tracks both external and internal temporal dynamics while updating integrated ontologies within a probabilistic semantic web infrastructure.

Collaborative datasets comprise ratings that connect two separate categories of entities: users and items. Previous research on such data has predominantly concentrated on filtering techniques aimed at estimating missing ratings for user-item combinations. This work addresses an alternative challenge: the visual representation of collaborative data. Our objective is to position both users and items as points within a shared Euclidean space, such that users are located proximate to items they have rated or would likely rate favorably, while maintaining distance from items they would rate unfavorably. We formulate this embedding problem as a continuous-valued nonlinear Bayesian network and apply Markov chain Monte Carlo and expectation maximization algorithms to derive the embedding solution. We introduce an evaluation metric for assessing visualization quality and benchmark our approach against local linear embedding and Eigentaste using three empirical datasets.

text: Markov Networks represent a fundamental tool in computer vision and machine learning applications. A particularly important category within this framework is Associative Markov Networks, which have demonstrated utility across numerous practical domains. For this network class, efficient computation of approximate optimal solutions is achievable through graph cut-based optimization techniques, such as alpha-expansion algorithms. An extension of this approach, termed the associative hierarchical network, has recently emerged as a natural extension to accommodate higher-order cliques beyond pairwise interactions. This generalized model proves particularly valuable for addressing object class segmentation tasks in computer vision. This work presents the associative hierarchical network formulation and introduces a computationally tractable graph cut-based inference algorithm. The proposed approach scales effectively to problems involving hundreds of thousands of variables with higher-order potentials spanning tens of thousands of variables per clique, a scale at which conventional linear programming approaches become impractical. We establish a 4-approximation bound for the general associative hierarchical network across arbitrary clique sizes, contributing to the limited body of existing approximation guarantees for Markov Network inference with higher-order cliques.

text: The automatic generation of textual descriptions for video content represents an important challenge in computer vision. While existing approaches, such as sequence-to-sequence architectures, have demonstrated effectiveness in producing general summaries of brief video sequences, generating precise and comprehensive captions for videos containing multiple nuanced actions remains a significant limitation. This work addresses this gap by introducing a hierarchical reinforcement learning approach to video captioning that employs a two-tier architecture: an upper-level Manager component responsible for establishing intermediate objectives, and a lower-level Worker component tasked with identifying elemental actions necessary to achieve these objectives. Through this stratified reinforcement mechanism operating across multiple levels of abstraction, the proposed method achieves substantial improvements over comparative baselines when evaluated on a recently developed large-scale benchmark for fine-grained video captioning. Additionally, the single-model variant of this approach attains competitive performance on the established MSR-VTT benchmark dataset.

text: Dictionary-based Cross-language Information Retrieval (CLIR) encounters significant obstacles, including polysemy in translation, absent vocabulary items in bilingual lexicons, and incomplete translation coverage. These challenges are particularly acute for agglutinative languages lacking robust stemming algorithms, where the absence of morphological variants in bilingual dictionaries substantially diminishes retrieval effectiveness. To address these limitations, this work presents a probabilistic framework for resolving translation ambiguity and generating plausible morphological variants of candidate terms. We introduce the Minimum Edit Support Candidates (MESC) technique, which leverages monolingual corpora alongside bilingual lexicons to convert queries from the source language into the target language of the document collection. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing dictionary-based methods in English-Persian CLIR tasks.

text: Dendritic cells (DCs), which constitute a component of the innate immune system capable of both enhancing and inhibiting immune responses, served as the biological inspiration for this computational model. The functional characteristics of human DCs were abstracted and formalized into an algorithmic framework designed for identifying anomalies. This approach was evaluated using a practical application: the real-time detection of port scanning activities. Our findings demonstrate that the simulated DC system exhibits notably distinct behavioral patterns when exposed to outgoing port scan traffic relative to its response to standard network processes.

text: Touch, as the first sensory modality to emerge during human development, serves as a fundamental component in our interactions with the physical world. Many object manipulation tasks depend on integrating tactile information to successfully execute desired actions, yet creating effective haptic feedback mechanisms remains a significant challenge. This study addresses manipulation tasks where tactile sensor data must inform adjustments to predetermined motion plans. To handle incomplete sensory information, we propose a framework that formulates the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process and learns an effective representation of haptic signals that functions as the state variable within this POMDP formulation. The approach employs deep recurrent neural networks as the underlying model architecture and applies variational Bayesian inference to refine the approximate posterior distribution. We extend deep Q-learning techniques to enable optimal action selection at each state without requiring access to a simulation environment. The proposed method is evaluated on a PR2 robotic platform across several instantiations of a rotary knob manipulation task that terminates upon auditory and tactile confirmation.

text: Non-negative matrix factorization approaches employing a hierarchical Gamma-Poisson framework effectively model user and item interactions in highly sparse datasets, making them well-suited for collaborative filtering tasks. Hierarchical Poisson factorization (HPF) has demonstrated particular promise for building scalable recommendation systems that handle extreme sparsity. Nevertheless, HPF exhibits a fundamental limitation: its sparsity mechanism (representing missing ratings) is tightly integrated with its response mechanism (representing observed rating magnitudes), constraining the flexibility of the latter component. We present hierarchical compound Poisson factorization (HCPF), which retains the computational benefits and Gamma-Poisson structure of HPF while scaling effectively to high-dimensional extremely sparse matrices. Crucially, HCPF separates the sparsity model from the response model, enabling the selection of the most appropriate probability distribution for the observed response values. This flexibility allows HCPF to accommodate binary, non-negative discrete, non-negative continuous, and zero-inflated continuous response types. Through evaluation on nine discrete and three continuous datasets, we demonstrate that HCPF more accurately characterizes the interplay between sparsity and response patterns compared to HPF.

text: Belief Propagation (BP) serves as a common approximation technique for performing exact probabilistic inference over graphical models, including Markov Random Fields (MRFs). Nevertheless, when graphs contain cycles, theoretical guarantees regarding BP's convergence remain unavailable in most scenarios. Previous research has addressed this limitation for MRFs where all edges possess identical symmetric, doubly stochastic potentials by proposing a linearized approximation of BP centered around baseline parameter values, demonstrating effectiveness for node classification tasks. This work extends these prior approaches by developing a method that reformulates loopy BP inference on arbitrary pairwise MRFs as the problem of solving a system of linear equations. The proposed method offers provable convergence properties alongside efficient matrix-based computation, while accommodating networks with heterogeneous edge characteristics. Empirical evaluation on synthetic networks with known edge potentials demonstrates that the linearized approach achieves classification performance comparable to standard BP when edge potentials are weak, simultaneously achieving substantial computational speedups in the inference process.
